title: The Wrenhaven Lily
tagline: Some clocks can only be set by other clocks.
intro: On the eve of the Winter Flower Show, the Wrenhaven Lily, an orchid that blooms once in seven years, was cut from the Park Glasshouse.
Penrose's last round was at a quarter past nine by the glasshouse clock. At six past ten, same clock, the door was forced. Lifting a lily takes six careful minutes.
Connie's advice: “If you can't check a clock against the church, check it against one you've mended.”

people.name: Ines Delacroix
people.blurb: Wintering her yacht at the Club. Her grandmother bred a white orchid in Roscoff once, and sold it when times were hard.

people.name: Bertram Cole
people.blurb: Doorman at the Grand, and runner-up for the orchid cup five years in a row. Says he's given up flowers.

people.name: Nell Garrow
people.blurb: Apprentice gardener at the Park since the autumn. The last person seen in the orchid house.

clocks.name: Yacht Club bar clock
clocks.note: The Commodore keeps it fast to hurry closing time.

clocks.name: Glasshouse clock
clocks.note: Old Penrose winds it on Sundays. It loses in a frost.

incident.title: The Wrenhaven Lily
incident.text: The prize orchid was cut from its pot in the Park Glasshouse. Last round 21:15, found broken into at 22:06, both by the glasshouse clock. Lifting it takes 6 minutes.

cards.title: Bar book
cards.text: Lights out all over the clubhouse. Candles on the tables. Back on in four minutes.

cards.title: Frost log
cards.text: Heaters tripped. Supply cut on the west feeder, back after four minutes. Thermometer held at 51°F.

cards.title: Coastguard log
cards.text: Radio check from the yacht Mouette at the Club moorings. Skipper: I. Delacroix.

cards.title: Radio book
cards.text: Mlle Delacroix called Hayle Head coastguard from the Club set. Signal good.

cards.title: Jory Tregear
cards.text: “Miss Delacroix sat by the window from nine by our clock until the lights went out at a quarter to ten. Then I lost sight of her for the candles.”
cards.firm: “Nine till the lights went, by the clock over the bar. I'm sure of it.”

cards.title: Bar tab
cards.text:
I. DELACROIX · 2 × hot toddy · settled
Timed off the clock over the bar.

cards.title: Exchange log
cards.text:
Yacht Club payphone → ROSCOFF, FRANCE
Trunk call · 4 minutes · caller “Delacroix”

cards.title: Ines Delacroix
cards.text: “I was at the Yacht Club from nine until long after eleven. In the bar, then on my boat at the Club moorings. I never went near the Park.”
cards.reply: “…The lily was my grandmother's. She bred it in Roscoff and sold it for bread in 1946. I walked to the Park when the lights went out. I have nothing more to say without a lawyer.”

cards.title: Gate book
cards.text:
Side gate unlatched and relatched. Visitor not signed in. (Woman's footprints in the frost, small boots. — A.P.)
Timed by the glasshouse clock.

cards.title: Left-luggage ticket
cards.text: One holdall deposited. Name: N. GARROW.

cards.title: Mr Penrose
cards.text: “Nell helped me pot up the cyclamen from twenty to nine until my last round at a quarter past. Then she was off to the station. Good girl, that one.”
cards.firm: “Twenty to nine till a quarter past, by the house clock. I've told you the truth, Detective.”

cards.title: Platform ticket
cards.text:
Platform ticket, 1d.
Clipped at the barrier: N. GARROW (staff pass, Park).

cards.title: Buffet chit
cards.text: Tea, Bath bun. On the Park's account: N. GARROW.

cards.title: Mr Hendy
cards.text: “Miss Garrow met the 22:25 from Truro. Young Davey Penhale. She'd been on that bench since half nine, nearly froze.”
cards.firm: “The 22:25 was three minutes late. She was there to meet it.”

cards.title: Bertram Cole
cards.text: “I was on the Grand's door from nine till gone eleven. Never left the step. I've given up orchids, whatever they say.”
cards.reply: “I nipped down the depot for a parcel off the Truro bus. Orchid compost. All right? I haven't given up. But I was back on the door by ten past ten, ask the taxi rank.”

cards.title: Night book
cards.text: Doorman on duty: B. COLE. Signed in.

cards.title: Parcel docket
cards.text: 1 parcel (sack, 28 lb) handed over at the depot. Signed: B. COLE.

cards.title: Exchange log
cards.text:
Grand Hotel front door → Wrenhaven Taxis · 1 minute
Caller: “Cole, on the door.”

triggers.question: Mr Penrose has Nell at the glasshouse from twenty to nine by his clock, yet she left a holdall at the station at 20:35, ten minutes' walk away. Is Penrose lying, or is his clock?
Cole swears he never left the Grand's door, but he signed for a parcel at the bus depot at 21:55.
The footprints at the Park gate can only be Ines's, and Ines says she never left the Yacht Club.

triggers.memo: The Yacht Club clock is seven minutes fast. And now its “lights out” is worth something: the Glasshouse's boiler logged the same power cut.
The glasshouse clock is nine minutes slow, and so was the crime: 21:24 to 22:15. Penrose was telling the truth all along.
Only one pair of small boots fits. They came from the Yacht Club.

memos.text: Two clocks tonight that nobody's ever checked. Mend the one you can. Then see what else it can mend.
Before you call Penrose a liar, look at whose clock he reads, and whether anything can set it.
Small boots, no name. Nobody fits yet, so something on the board is still wrong. Probably a clock.

reconstruction: 21:40. The lights go out at the Yacht Club. Ines slips away in the dark.
21:52. A hot toddy settled at the bar, timed by a clock seven minutes fast. Then out into the frost.
22:03. The Park's side gate. Penrose's clock says 21:54, nine minutes slow.
22:04. Six careful minutes with a pruning knife and a hatbox.
22:22. Back at the Club payphone, calling Roscoff: “Elle rentre à la maison.”
epilogue: The lily was in a hatbox in the Mouette's forward cabin, wrapped in a jumper and still in bloom. Ines had meant to sail for Roscoff on the morning tide.

The Flower Show committee, after a long and heated meeting, sent the Lily to the Roscoff botanical garden on loan, with a brass plate in her grandmother's name. Cole won the orchid cup at last and cried a little.
Penrose bought a new clock. Connie's note: “Five for five, partner. A clock you've mended is as good as the church. Merry Christmas.”
